title: Transformer Overview
definition: A Transformer is a neural sequence architecture that builds context-aware token representations purely through self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers — no recurrence, no convolution — stacked with residual connections and layer normalization to make deep, fully parallel training practical.
summary: Introduced in "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017), the Transformer alternates multi-head self-attention (every token gathers information from every other token in one step) with position-wise feed-forward sublayers, wrapped in residual connections and layer norm for stable, deep training. Because attention is permutation-invariant, position must be injected explicitly (sinusoidal or learned position embeddings added to the token embeddings). Nearly every modern LLM (GPT, Llama, Claude, etc.) uses only the decoder half — a single causal self-attention stack — trained to predict the next token.
objectives: Explain how self-attention turns static token embeddings into context-aware representations via Q/K/V projections and softmax weighting.
State why dot products are scaled by `√d_k`, and what silently breaks if you skip it.
Contrast encoder-decoder vs. decoder-only Transformers and why LLMs standardized on decoder-only.
Reason about self-attention's `O(n²)` time/memory cost and its production consequences (context-length limits, KV-cache growth).
Spot common production bugs: causal-mask errors and their (non-obvious) symptoms.
lesson:
Token embeddings give each token a fixed vector — "bank" gets the same vector whether it means a riverbank or a financial institution. Self-attention's job is to make that vector *contextual* by letting every token pull information from every other token, weighted by relevance.

Mechanically, each embedding `x_i` is projected through three learned matrices:

```
q_i = W_Q x_i      k_i = W_K x_i      v_i = W_V x_i
attn(i,j) = softmax_j( (q_i · k_j) / sqrt(d_k) )
output_i  = Σ_j attn(i,j) * v_j
```

Every token does this simultaneously — that's the structural break from RNNs, which update a hidden state one token at a time. Because any two tokens interact in a single attention step (`O(1)` path length), Transformers don't suffer the vanishing-gradient decay that makes RNNs weak at long-range dependencies (RNN path length is `O(n)`).

Multi-head attention runs several of these projections in parallel, each into a smaller subspace (`d_model / h` per head), so different heads can specialize — one might track syntax, another coreference — then concatenates and linearly projects back to `d_model`. Each attention sublayer sits inside a residual connection with layer norm (`x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x))` in most modern models) — this is what makes stacking dozens of blocks trainable at all; without the residual path, gradients through that many layers of attention and feed-forward math would vanish or blow up. A position-wise feed-forward network (expand ~4x, nonlinearity, project back) follows each attention sublayer, adding per-token nonlinear capacity — it holds most of the parameters in a typical Transformer.

**Key gotcha:** the `√d_k` scaling isn't cosmetic. Dot products of two random `d_k`-dimensional vectors grow in magnitude with `d_k`; unscaled, they push softmax into a saturated regime where gradients vanish and training stalls — easy to break silently if you ever hand-roll attention. The second common production gotcha is an off-by-one in the causal mask: it won't crash or NaN, and may even look fine in training loss, but it either leaks future tokens (making the task artificially easy) or blocks legitimate self-attention (degrading quality) — always unit-test a hand-rolled mask against a tiny known sequence.
examples:
**Example 1 — attention by hand** (2 tokens, `d_k=2`, identity projections so `q=k=v=x`):

```
tokens: "the" -> x1 = [1, 0]      "cat" -> x2 = [0, 1]

score(the, the) = q1·k1 = 1
score(the, cat) = q1·k2 = 0
scaled by 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707:      [0.707, 0]

softmax([0.707, 0]) ≈ [0.670, 0.330]

output_the = 0.670*v1 + 0.330*v2
           = 0.670*[1,0] + 0.330*[0,1]
           = [0.670, 0.330]
```

"the"'s new representation is 67% itself + 33% "cat" — that blend *is* contextualization.

**Example 2 — verify it in code:**

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0],    # "the"
                   [0.0, 1.0]])  # "cat"
q = k = v = x                    # identity projections, for illustration
d_k = q.shape[-1]

scores  = q @ k.T / d_k ** 0.5
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
out     = weights @ v

print(weights)
# tensor([[0.6698, 0.3302],
#         [0.3302, 0.6698]])
```

Matches the hand calculation. In practice `W_Q/W_K/W_V` are learned (not identity), everything is batched over `(batch, heads, seq_len, d_k)`, and production code runs a fused kernel (`F.scaled_dot_product_attention`, FlashAttention) instead of materializing the full `seq × seq` score matrix.
tradeoffs: Self-attention is `O(n²)` in time and memory in sequence length `n` — every token scores against every other token — versus an RNN's `O(n)` but strictly sequential compute. You trade extra FLOPs/memory for full parallelism during training and `O(1)` path length between any two tokens (better long-range modeling, no recurrent gradient decay). At inference, autoregressive decoding needs a growing KV cache (memory ∝ `sequence_length × layers × heads × d_k`), which — not attention's FLOPs — is usually the real production bottleneck for long-context serving; mitigations include grouped/multi-query attention (fewer KV heads), FlashAttention-style fused kernels (less memory traffic, same FLOPs), or sparse/sliding-window attention (fewer than `n²` pairs) for very long context. For short sequences, tight latency budgets, or streaming with little need for long-range context, a smaller architecture (RNN, CNN, linear attention) can beat a full Transformer on cost without losing much quality.

diagnosticQuiz.q: What best defines the mechanism that lets a Transformer build context-aware token representations from static token embeddings?
choices: A convolution sliding over a fixed-size local window of embeddings
A larger embedding table that already encodes every possible context
Self-attention: each token computes a weighted sum over all tokens' value vectors, weighted by query–key similarity
A recurrent hidden state that updates sequentially, one token at a time
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: Self-attention is precisely this operation — project into queries/keys/values, then softmax-weighted mixing across all positions. Option A describes an RNN and option C a CNN; option D reflects the common misconception that embeddings themselves encode context, when in fact token embeddings are static and it's the attention layers built on top that make them contextual.

diagnosticQuiz.q: In scaled dot-product attention, `softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)V`, why divide by `√d_k` specifically?
choices: To counteract dot products growing in magnitude with `d_k`, which would otherwise push softmax into a low-gradient saturated regime
To implement the causal mask correctly
To make each token's attention weights sum to 1
To match the output dimension to the value vectors' dimension
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: For vectors with roughly unit-variance components, a dot product's variance scales with `d_k`, so larger `d_k` produces larger-magnitude scores that saturate softmax and shrink gradients — the `√d_k` divisor keeps scores in a well-behaved range. Softmax summing to 1 (A) holds regardless of scaling, and the scaling has nothing to do with value dimensions or masking.

diagnosticQuiz.q: Why does a Transformer typically handle long-range dependencies (e.g., agreement between words 60 tokens apart) better than a vanilla RNN?
choices: Positional encodings memorize the exact word order during training
Any two tokens interact through a single attention step — an `O(1)` path length — versus an RNN's `O(n)` sequential path where signal decays
It uses a larger vocabulary
It has strictly more trainable parameters
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: The number of computation steps information must cross between two tokens drives long-range performance: attention connects any pair directly in one step, while an RNN propagates signal through every intermediate step, where it's prone to vanishing/exploding gradients. Parameter count and vocabulary size (A, C) aren't the mechanism, and positional encodings (D) convey word order, not long-range dependency resolution.

diagnosticQuiz.q: Your production system must serve 100k+-token documents, and full self-attention's `O(n²)` cost is the main latency/memory bottleneck. What's the most directly relevant fix?
choices: Use sparse/sliding-window attention or an IO-aware exact kernel (e.g., FlashAttention) to cut the effective attention cost
Remove layer normalization to speed up each forward pass
Add more attention heads at the same total dimension
Switch the training loss from cross-entropy to MSE
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: Sparse/windowed attention reduces the number of token pairs scored, and FlashAttention reduces memory traffic (not FLOPs) by avoiding materializing the full `n×n` score matrix — both are standard, targeted responses to the quadratic-cost bottleneck. Changing the loss function or head count doesn't touch attention's asymptotic cost, and removing LayerNorm destabilizes training/inference while barely denting the real bottleneck.

diagnosticQuiz.q: In a decoder-only LLM, what's the most likely symptom of an off-by-one bug in the causal attention mask?
choices: Training immediately produces NaN loss
The model trains more slowly but reaches the same final quality
Training loss looks normal (or artificially low) but generation quality degrades, because the model learned to use information — like future tokens — that won't exist at inference time
Positional encodings are silently set to zero
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: Causal-mask bugs are dangerous precisely because they're silent: leaking a future token makes next-token prediction artificially easy (loss looks great) while generation breaks, since future tokens genuinely don't exist at inference time; the reverse bug (blocking legitimate self-attention) just quietly degrades quality. It doesn't reliably crash training with NaNs (A), doesn't just slow convergence with no quality impact (C), and has no direct relation to positional encodings (D).

interviewQuestions.q: Walk me through what happens inside one Transformer block, and why each piece (attention, residual, LayerNorm, FFN) needs to be there.
interviewQuestions.a: Input is token embeddings + positional encoding. Then: LayerNorm → multi-head self-attention → add residual; LayerNorm → position-wise FFN (expand ~4x, nonlinearity, project back) → add residual. Attention mixes information across positions (context); the FFN adds per-token nonlinear capacity and holds most of the parameters; residual connections are what make 30–100+ stacked layers trainable at all — without them, gradients through that many sublayers vanish or explode; LayerNorm keeps activation scales stable layer to layer so the residual stream stays well-conditioned as depth grows.

interviewQuestions.q: Why does the KV cache matter for LLM inference cost, and how does it connect to attention?
interviewQuestions.a: Generating token `t` needs attention over keys/values for every token `< t`. Recomputing K/V for the whole prefix at each new token would cost `O(n²)` total; caching each layer's K/V per generated token turns that into `O(n)` — the standard optimization in every production LLM server. This shifts the cost from compute to memory: cache size grows with `sequence_length × layers × heads × head_dim`, and at long context or large batch size that memory footprint — not attention's FLOPs — is usually the real serving bottleneck, which is why grouped/multi-query attention (shared KV heads) and cache quantization are common production levers.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do essentially all modern LLMs use a decoder-only Transformer instead of the original encoder-decoder design?
interviewQuestions.a: Decoder-only with causal self-attention directly matches the pretraining objective that made LLMs scale: next-token prediction over raw, unpaired text. The original encoder-decoder split existed for supervised sequence-to-sequence tasks (e.g., translation) needing a separate "read the full input first" pass. A decoder-only model still handles translation-like or conditional tasks fine — the "input" just goes in the prompt, and causal self-attention conditions on it (in-context learning) — while simplifying the architecture to one attention type and one stack, which scales more simply.
